prompt.context: You are an MBA2 student. You walk into your apartment and find a baby dinosaur in the corner of your room. The dinosaur is the only one in the world, and it turns out he is friendly. No other information is available.
prompt.question: What do you do?

clarifying_info.q: Is the dinosaur dangerous or aggressive?
Is there anyone else who knows about the dinosaur?
clarifying_info.a: No other information is available — you are the only one who knows.

framework: Initial reaction / decision tree: Take action (run, call 911, call family/friends, arm yourself) vs. take no-action (wait to see if it leaves, assess friendliness first)
Assess the dinosaur: friendly vs. not friendly — determine safety before proceeding
If friendly, decide: monetize vs. non-monetizing uses (research, personal companion, donate to science)
If monetizing: sell the dinosaur outright vs. build a business/franchise around it
Business options: lease to zoo, star in a movie, entertainment show, create an ecosystem (theme park)
Risk assessment: dinosaur death, dinosaur attacks spectators, government seizure, environmental/legal concerns
Hedging strategy against key risks, especially dinosaur death

questions.prompt: What are possible ways to monetize or make money from the dinosaur?
questions.guidance: Candidate should distinguish between selling the dinosaur outright (one-time transaction) versus building a recurring business. Strong answers include: licensing/leasing to a zoo, starring in a movie or entertainment show, creating an ecosystem such as a theme park or franchise. Candidate should also mention non-monetizing alternatives (research, science donation) to show structured thinking.

questions.prompt: Would you prefer to sell the dinosaur or use it for a business? Why? What are the possible costs and revenues in each case?
questions.guidance: Sell: simple, immediate cash, no operational risk, but one-time upside and no control. Business: higher long-term upside, recurring revenue (tickets, merchandise, licensing), but requires capital, operational expertise, and carries ongoing risk. A strong candidate will compare NPV of each path qualitatively and argue for the business option given the dinosaur's uniqueness and scarcity value.

questions.prompt: What are the potential risks in this situation?
questions.guidance: Key risk categories: (1) Dinosaur health — it could die, eliminating the asset; (2) Safety — dinosaur attacks or injures spectators, creating liability; (3) Legal/regulatory — government could seize the dinosaur and claim ownership rights; (4) Environmental — unknown ecological impact of a living dinosaur; (5) Reputational/ethical — public controversy around exploiting a unique living creature.

questions.prompt: What are possible ways to hedge against the possibility of dinosaur death?
questions.guidance: Strong answers include: (1) Obtain insurance on the dinosaur; (2) Clone the dinosaur using modern genetic technology; (3) Consult paleontologists and veterinary scientists for care guidance; (4) Build an ecosystem (theme park, movie franchise) that generates IP and brand value independent of the live dinosaur, so the business survives even if the dinosaur does not.

brainstorming.prompt: What are all the possible ways to monetize or build a business around the baby dinosaur?

categories.name: Entertainment & Media
ideas: Star in a TV show or documentary
Feature in a live entertainment show or circus

categories.name: Ecosystem / Theme Park
ideas: License the brand for merchandise (toys, clothing, games)

categories.name: Research & Science
ideas: Lease to a university or research institution
Partner with biotech firms for cloning research

categories.name: Hedging / Risk Mitigation
ideas: Build brand/IP independent of the live animal
Seek government partnership for protection and legitimacy

recommendation: Create an ecosystem (theme park or entertainment franchise) around the dinosaur to maximize long-term value, given it is the only one in the world — its scarcity makes one-time sale a massive underutilization of the asset
Build brand and IP around the dinosaur so the business retains value even if the dinosaur dies
risks: Dinosaur dies before the business is established
Government or regulatory body seizes the dinosaur and claims ownership
Dinosaur injures or kills spectators, creating legal liability
Environmental or ethical backlash limits business operations
next_steps: Conduct a feasibility study for creating a theme park or entertainment ecosystem
Consult legal experts on ownership rights and regulatory requirements
Engage veterinary and paleontological experts to assess the dinosaur's health and care needs
Explore cloning and insurance options to hedge against asset loss
